# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

insights.line: What would have made a difference

whys.g1: The two answers are about different things -- one sizes jobs by profiling a short test run, the other says sizing is fine and the real pain is data staging and library mismatches -- so leaving each on its own is how I'd read them, and no group exists that either should have gone into.
whys.g2: There is no junk on this line; both answers are on-topic replies from people who run jobs on the cluster, so nothing was let into a group that shouldn't be.

whys.g1: Hiroshi's short test run and Kwabena's sizes from last week's runs are both people already sizing from their own runs, the name says that plainly, and Claire's closed binary and Diego's fear of losing days to a cut walltime are separate reasons that rightly stay out of that group.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; all four say why a sizing tool would be too much for them.

founder.order_why: It runs from where the idea applies, to the problem, to my solution and its fit, advantage and adoption cost, to the pilot and sending, which is how I'd explain Expanse to a researcher on a SLURM cluster.

screens.why4: It's a free-text box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a founder who doesn't want to test relative advantage.
screens.why5: My two benefits are kept word for word, but the belief line 'it would have made their last job submission better' blurs them into a generic 'better' that no longer says runs first time or waits less in the queue.
screens.instead: Keep the question; make the belief: 'For most, their last job would have run to the end first time, or waited less in the queue, with a sized request.'

screens.why1: Straight after I typed what it does better, Keel shows me the two advantages it drew and the belief it will test, the obvious next check before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The rows are in my researchers' words (resubmits, the wait in the queue), but "made their last job submission better" is vague: better how, the run finishing or the wait?
screens.why3: A researcher knows whether their last job died mid-run or sat in the queue, so they can judge whether right-sized requests would have helped it.
screens.why4: The two rows are my two advantages, distinct and in the trade's words: a job that runs to the end first time, and a smaller request that fits sooner.
screens.why5: The rows keep what I typed, but the belief flattens them into a generic "better" and pins it to the last submission, which with several a day may be a tiny test job that gains nothing.
screens.instead: Belief: For most, sizes set from a prediction would have let their last real run (not a quick test) finish first time or start sooner; rows: Jobs that run to the end first time, no resubmits / A shorter wait in the queue for a smaller request

screens.why1: After how it fits and what it does better, asking what researchers must do to start using it is the natural last solution question.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps and learning are plain words to me, and 'padding' in the belief is exactly how we talk about over-requesting.
screens.why3: I know what a researcher changes: they stop padding their requests and apply the line-level fixes, since the agent and scheduler hook are the operator's install, not theirs.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who has nothing to test here.
screens.why5: Keel's belief keeps the suggested sizes instead of padding but drops my second step, applying the line-level code fixes it suggests.
screens.instead: Keep the question; have the belief say 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding, and apply the code fixes it suggests', or ask me which of the two to test.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what they'd have to do to start, Keel shows the adoption steps it drew and the one belief it will test, which is the natural check point.
screens.why2: Padding, suggested sizes and line-level code fixes are how my researchers and I talk about submit scripts; I read it once.
screens.why3: Whether a researcher would trust our sizes over their own padding is exactly the thing I know and worry about from the thread.
screens.why4: The two rows are mine and distinct, but the step that comes before both, letting the agent read their job script and source code, is missing, and it's the first thing they actually have to accept.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my point that the hard part is giving up the padding, with 'most' as my honest reading of it.
screens.instead: Rows: Let it read the job script and source code before submit / Use the suggested sizes instead of padding / Apply the line-level code fixes it suggests -- belief: Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding.

screens.why1: After writing down what researchers must do to start, picking the one adoption step to test is the obvious next move, and the suggested sizes instead of padding is the heart of the bet.
screens.why2: Padding, suggested sizes and line-level code fixes are how I and my researchers talk about job requests, so it reads on the first pass.
screens.why3: I know from the measured cluster and the thread that dropping the 2-3x padding is the real hurdle, so I can pick this from what I know.
screens.why4: The two items are distinct and in my words, but there is no chip for a third step I named (letting the agent sit on the node and read their scripts), so a founder whose real hurdle is trust has nowhere to pick it.
screens.why5: The belief and the bar say what I typed: most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding, held if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious place to try it on a few people and lock what I believe, and it follows straight on from the solution checks.
screens.why2: To me "the pilot" is the paid pilot I sell to a department after the two-week measurement, so a bare "The pilot" headline makes me read twice before I see it means a trial run of Keel's study, and "freezes your beliefs" is Keel's word, not mine.
screens.why3: Deciding when my own study is ready to send is squarely mine to answer.
screens.why4: The screen shows only a Continue action, no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: Nothing of my problem, solution or roles is changed or shown here; it is Keel's own step.
screens.instead: Try the study on a few people first: locking fixes what you believe and writes the questions strangers will be asked. [Continue]

screens.why1: Picking who runs the interviews belongs in the last step before strangers see the study, right after the pilot, so I see why it is asked here.
screens.why2: "Needs Keel's credits" and "links go out as text" make me read twice: I can't tell if text means the fallback without the AI or how every link is sent, and "the face" for an interviewer is Keel's word, not mine.
screens.why3: Whether I want an AI voice or a plain text survey for researchers on SLURM clusters is my call, and I can make it.
screens.why4: The only choice I can see is locking the face Keel preselected; the other paths (no AI, text only, or picking another face) aren't spelled out as options beside it.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my wording is rewritten here, and no roles leak; it is a setting about the study, not about Expanse.
screens.instead: Who will interview the researchers? — An AI voice interviewer (uses Keel credits) / A text-only survey sent as a link (no credits); then, if AI: keep the interviewer Keel picked, or choose another.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers answer belongs right before sending, after the pilot and the interviewer screens.
screens.why2: The AI interviewer line is garbled: 'Every answer in a quiet room. More than 90% in loud places down to 5 dB.Hear it' reads like two broken claims run together, and I have to reread it to work out that it means transcription accuracy.
screens.why3: I know my researchers sit at a terminal and will tap through text, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct, but the AI option's description is mangled (the run-on accuracy claim, the odd '5 dB', the missing space before 'Hear it'), which makes it read oddly beside the clean text option.
screens.why5: My pick, Text only, is shown as I made it, and nothing about Expanse leaks into the options.
screens.instead: How should they answer? — AI interviewer: a face on video asks each question aloud; they answer by talking or tapping (understood more than 90% of the time even in noisy rooms) · Text only: they read each question and tap · Let them choose: they pick the interviewer or text when they open the link

screens.why1: A gate on cluster size makes sense first, but it never asks whether I submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster at all, and the kicker's "A recent time" doesn't match a question with no occasion in it.
screens.why2: "Do you have" stops me: I personally have an allocation of maybe eight GPUs, while the shared cluster I submit to has hundreds, and "available" could mean idle right now or just existing.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our cluster is, but I'd be guessing whether "you" means me, my lab or the whole cluster, and whether "available" means free GPUs on a given day.
screens.why4: Yes and No are distinct, but my true answer, "the cluster I use has that many, but they're not mine," fits neither cleanly.
screens.why5: The founder's segment is researchers working on clusters of 100 or more GPUs, but the screen asks whether the respondent has 100 GPUs, so a researcher in the target segment who answers honestly could be screened out.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes, SLURM; Yes, Kubernetes; Yes, something else; or No.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a big shared cluster, asking whether I actually sized a job this week is the obvious next gate.
screens.why2: I'd say I set or requested memory, GPUs and wall time in my sbatch or pod spec, not that I guessed them, so the word makes me stop and wonder whether copying last week's script counts.
screens.why3: I submit jobs every day and know exactly what I put in the request.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but a gate should carry no escape and this one carries two, one of them "I'd rather not say"; the No also mixes "didn't submit anything" with "reused old settings without thinking".
screens.why5: "Guess" is the founder's framing of my situation pushed into my mouth, a slight lean toward the problem they want me to have.
screens.why6: Short, one question, the three resources are a list I can hold, and "Yes or no" closes it cleanly.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you submit a job where you had to set its memory, GPUs and time limit yourself? Yes / No

screens.why1: After the two questions about guessing my job's memory, GPUs and run time, showing an idea that predicts those is the obvious next step for Part 2.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, submission script, GPU memory and walltime are my everyday words, so I get it on first reading, though 'GPU memory, memory' makes me pause for a second.
screens.why3: I submit jobs with scripts and guessed resources every week, so I can picture this tool on my own runs.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose, in plain terms of my own work, and nothing about the founder's roles or plans leaks beyond the idea itself.
screens.why6: Said aloud, the six-item list 'predicted GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime, failure warnings and line-level suggestions' is a mouthful, 'memory, memory' sounds like a stutter, and the belief line mostly repeats what the tool shows.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse. When you submit a job on SLURM or Kubernetes, it reads your code, your submission script and the hardware, then tells you the GPU memory, CPU memory, CPUs and walltime the job will need. It also warns you before a job is likely to fail and suggests which lines of code to change.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card it's plausible Expanse needs to see my code, but nothing tells me why where my code lives matters, so it lands abruptly as the first idea question.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but 'sitting on the cluster' is loose: on SLURM my code is on the shared filesystem, while on Kubernetes it's baked into a container image or cloned at job start, and I'd pause over which of those counts.
screens.why3: I know exactly where the code for my last fine-tuning run lived, so this is about my own submission.
screens.why4: 'Mostly' and 'Partly' blur into each other and mean little for source code, and the common true answers 'in a container image' or 'pulled from git when the job starts' are missing.
screens.why5: It seems to stand in for whether the tool can read my job to estimate memory, GPUs and run time, but asking about the code's location exposes a product mechanism rather than whether it fits how I submit jobs.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, four one-word options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last job submission. Where was the code it ran? Options: on the cluster's shared filesystem; in a container image; pulled from git when the job started; on my laptop, copied over. Escape: I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about my last submission, asking whether Expanse would have made that time better is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The question reads easily, but "made things better" is vague about which things: my job, my wait, or the cluster, so I would pause on it.
screens.why3: I can say whether my last job died from under-requesting, but whether a tool I have only seen on a card would have fixed it is partly a guess.
screens.why4: Two of the options are reasons it would be better (jobs that run first time, shorter queue wait), not answers to better-or-not, so they overlap "It would have made things better" and I cannot tell which one to pick when both apply.
screens.why5: "Jobs that run first time, no resubmits" and "A shorter wait in the queue" read like the founder's pitch handed to me as answers rather than my own words, though the idea card itself is shown on purpose.
screens.why6: Hearing "It would have made things better" and then two benefits followed by "No difference" is hard to hold, because the list mixes a verdict scale with reasons and sounds like two questions in one breath.
screens.instead: Think of your last job: would Expanse have made it go better, or not? A lot better; a little better; no different; worse. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After the idea card and whether Expanse would have helped, asking if I'd actually take its suggested requests over my own padding is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: I pad requests all the time so 'padding' is my word, but 'suggested sizes' made me stop for a second: sizes of what, memory, GPUs, wall time?
screens.why3: I decide on every submission whether to trust a lower number or pad it, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' misses my real condition: I'd switch only if the suggestions didn't get my jobs killed mid-run, which is about trust, not worth.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of right-sizing requests instead of over-reserving, and nothing beyond the named card leaks in.
screens.why6: It is short and says well aloud: one question and four short options I can hold, with the escape said last.
screens.instead: Would you submit with Expanse's suggested memory, GPUs and run time instead of padding them, or not? Yes; Yes, once I'd seen it not get jobs killed; Probably not; No; or I can't tell.
